nameStory: Mintweed gets its name from being part of the mint family, though it's actually a sage rather than a true mint. The 'weed' part comes from its weedy nature - it pops up in disturbed areas and spreads readily where conditions are right. Some folks also call it lanceleaf sage because of its narrow, spear-shaped leaves.
description: Mintweed is a small annual plant that grows between 4 to 28 inches tall, looking somewhat scraggly and branched. It has narrow, pointed leaves arranged in pairs along square stems - a telltale sign of the mint family. Small pale to dark blue flowers appear in circular clusters (called whorls) around the stem during summer and fall. Despite its weedy appearance, those delicate blue blooms can be quite pretty up close.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves up to 2 inches long arranged in opposite pairs along the stem - they feel slightly fuzzy and have a subtle sage-like scent when crushed

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny pale blue to dark blue flowers arranged in distinct circular clusters (whorls) around the square stem at regular intervals

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Bushy annual plant reaching 4-28 inches with multiple branching stems that feel distinctly square when rolled between your fingers

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Small, dark nutlets develop after flowering - typical of the mint family, these tiny seeds can persist and help identify the plant even after blooming ends

habitat: In New England, mintweed is quite rare with only 7 recorded observations, typically found in disturbed areas like roadsides, abandoned lots, or edge habitats. It prefers open, sunny spots with well-drained soil and often appears where the ground has been disturbed. Look for it in areas that might remind you of western prairies - dry, open spaces with poor to moderate soil.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small rosettes with the characteristic narrow leaves becoming visible in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Plants grow rapidly and begin producing their distinctive whorled blue flowers in mid to late summer.
seasonality.fall: Flowering continues into early fall, followed by seed production. Plants begin to look scraggly and brown as they complete their annual cycle.
seasonality.winter: Dead stems and seed heads may persist into winter, but the annual plants have died back completely.

funFact: This innocent-looking little plant can actually be toxic to livestock due to nitrate accumulation - cattle, sheep, and goats can get sick from eating it, especially in hay, though poisoning cases are quite rare and require consuming large amounts.
confusionNotes: Mintweed might be confused with other small blue-flowered plants, but the combination of square stems, opposite narrow leaves, and whorled flower arrangement is distinctive. Remember: 'Square stems and whorled blooms = mint family room!'
contextualKnowledge: Though called 'mintweed,' this plant is actually a sage (Salvia species) rather than a true mint, showing how common names can be misleading. It's native to western North America and quite rare in New England, likely appearing as an occasional introduction rather than an established population.
compareHints: Unlike other sages that might be found in New England gardens like lyreleaf sage (which has much broader, lobed leaves), mintweed has very narrow, simple leaves and a weedy appearance. Most other Salvia species you'll encounter are either cultivated garden plants with showier flowers or have distinctly different leaf shapes and growth habits.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike lyreleaf sage which has distinctive lobed basal leaves and prefers shady woods, giant blue sage has narrow, unlobed leaves and demands full sun.
Unlike native New England sages like lyreleaf sage, chia is much taller and more robust, growing 3-5 feet compared to the 1-2 foot height of most regional relatives.
Unlike our native Lyreleaf Sage which has deeply lobed leaves and purple flowers, Sticky Sage has simple heart-shaped leaves and yellow flowers.
Lyreleaf sage is the only Salvia species you're likely to encounter in New England, making it unique in the region.
Unlike the native lyreleaf sage with its small purple flowers and basal rosette of leaves, anise-scented sage forms tall bushy plants with much larger, intensely blue flowers.
